title: Canaries Dashboard: employment by age and AI-exposure quintile
measure: ADP payroll employment index (Nov 2022 = 100) by age band and AI-exposure fifth of occupations; annualised % change by gender
latest_value: Ages 22–25, most exposed: 87.2 (Aug 2026); women −4.5%/yr, men −2.5%/yr since Nov 2022 (to Jul 2026); page last updated 23 Sep 2026
finding: Employment of 22–25 year olds in the most AI-exposed occupations is about 13% below Nov 2022 while same-age workers in the least exposed occupations are about 8% above it.
limits: AI exposure not use; ADP firms not random; five-year balanced panel excludes new firms

title: KI-indeksen: monthly employment by AI exposure, Norway
measure: Private-sector employment index (Nov 2022 = 100) by AI-exposure quintile and age band (21–30 … 51–60), A-ordningen register data via SSB
latest_value: Values only in charts; text: AI index 'about zero'; ages 21–30 in most exposed occupations have fallen relative to young workers elsewhere and older workers in same jobs
finding: A full-population register replication of the Canaries design finds no overall effect but a fall for 21–30 year olds in the most exposed occupations.
limits: no numbers in page text; exposure not use; 40% of private jobs in top two quintiles vs 66% in US ADP

title: AI Labor Market Tracker (monthly)
measure: Gap in job postings between most and least AI-exposed occupations; headcount event studies by age from weighted online profiles
latest_value: Postings gap −29% (Sep 2026), narrowing from −40% (Jul 2026); next release 5 Nov 2026
finding: The postings gap between most- and least-exposed occupations narrowed from −40% to −29% between July and September 2026.
limits: vendor data, unpublished weights; LLM-scored exposure; only a few releases

title: RPLS August 2026 release: employment in AI-exposed jobs for workers 22–25
measure: Relative headcount gap, workers 22–25 in most vs least AI-exposed occupations since Nov 2022
latest_value: 19% gap for ages 22–25; all ages about −6% (Aug 2026)
finding: Revelio reports 22–25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs 19% behind those in the least exposed, close to the Stanford figure.
limits: read via press-release reprint; release text internally inconsistent on jobs added

title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
measure: Occupational-mix dissimilarity since ChatGPT vs past tech waves; unemployment by AI exposure and usage; synthetic diff-in-diff (CPS)
latest_value: 'not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI' (updated 15 Sep 2026)
finding: The economy-wide occupational mix shows no clear AI footprint, and AI usage measures show no link to employment or unemployment changes.
limits: CPS too small for age×occupation cells; blunt economy-wide measure

title: Employment rate, ages 25–54 (LNS12300060)
measure: Employment-population ratio, ages 25–54 (%)
finding: Prime-age employment is at or above its pre-ChatGPT level (79.8% Nov 2022).
limits: economy-wide; population controls revised each January

title: Job Cuts Report: cuts attributed to AI
measure: Announced US job cuts where employer cites AI (count, share)
latest_value: 3,961 in Sep 2026 (about 9% of 43,281); 120,136 YTD (about 21%), still top reason YTD
finding: AI-attributed announced cuts reached about a fifth of 2026 cuts but fell back to under 4,000 a month in Aug–Sep.
limits: employers' stated reasons; announcements not separations; possible AI-washing

title: Software development job postings on Indeed (IHLIDXUSTPSOFTDEVE)
measure: Postings index, 1 Feb 2020 = 100, SA, 7-day average
finding: Software postings are about two-thirds below their Feb 2022 peak, most of the fall having come before ChatGPT, and have edged up from a late-2024 low of about 68.
limits: all experience levels; one platform; adverts not hires

title: The Labor Market Is Tilting Toward Seniority
measure: Postings classified Entry (0–1 yrs) / Mid (2–4) / Senior (5+) by text classifier; % change y/y and vs Jan 2025
latest_value: Senior +14.7% y/y, entry −7.5% y/y (May 2026); entry share of software postings 4.5% (Q1 2026)
finding: Senior postings rose about 15% in the year to May 2026 while entry-level postings fell 7.5%; tech's senior share rose 9 points 2019–25.
limits: classifier-based; blog post not public series; author does not attribute to AI

cite: Federal Reserve Bank of New York 2026
title: The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates
measure: Unemployment and underemployment rates, bachelor's holders aged 22–27 (%)
finding: Recent-graduate unemployment has held at about 5.6% for three quarters, above the all-worker rate, with underemployment edging up to 42%.
limits: not tied to AI; graduates' disadvantage began about 2019

title: Unemployment rate, bachelor's holders aged 20–24 (CGBD2024) vs 25+ (CGBD25O)
measure: Unemployment rate (%), NSA monthly; gap in points (derived Jan–Sep averages)
latest_value: Jan–Sep 2026 average 6.8% vs 3.1% (gap 3.7 pts), down from 4.4 pts in Jan–Sep 2025
finding: The young-graduate unemployment gap widened from 3.4 points (2022) to 4.4 (2025), then narrowed to 3.7 in 2026 as older graduates' unemployment rose.
limits: small CPS cells, NSA, derived averages; not tied to AI

title: Employed persons by NACE Rev. 2, ages 15–24 vs 25–64, information and communication (J), EU27
measure: Employed persons (thousands), quarterly, not seasonally adjusted
finding: EU under-25 employment in information and communication fell 15% from 2023 to 2025 (annual averages) while 25–64 employment in the sector rose 4.7% and all under-25 employment was flat.
limits: sector not occupation; boom-bust (2025 back to 2021 level); NSA; 2021 break

title: Youth employment amidst cooling labour demand (Economic Bulletin 5/2026, box)
measure: Youth/total unemployment ratio; youth employment by sector; Okun's-law residuals (euro area)
finding: Euro-area youth employment fell 18.6% in ICT, 5.3% in professional and 3.1% in financial services (Q1 2023–Q1 2026), and the youth/total unemployment ratio rose from 2.1 to 2.4; the ECB says this cannot yet be attributed to AI or remote work.
limits: descriptive; no AI exposure measure

title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion (BTOS AI supplement)
measure: Share of firms using AI; share reporting AI-related employment decreases
latest_value: 18% of firms use AI (32% employment-weighted); 2% report AI-related employment decreases (Nov 2025–Jan 2026)
finding: AI-related employment decreases were reported by only 2% of US firms; 66% of AI users only augment tasks.
limits: self-report; headcount not age; supplement wording changes

title: ISE Student Recruitment Survey 2025
measure: Graduate vacancies at member employers (% change y/y); applications per vacancy
latest_value: Graduate vacancies −8% (2024/25); 140 applications per vacancy; apprentices +8%
finding: UK graduate hiring at large employers fell 8% in 2024/25, the first fall since 2020, while applications per vacancy hit a record 140.
limits: 155 member employers; not tied to AI; ISE commentary attributes fall mainly to public-sector cuts

title: The graduate jobs market isn't collapsing
measure: Graduate Outcomes survey (15 months after graduation): share of employed graduates in professional-level roles
finding: UK graduates in professional-level jobs dipped 1 point to 70.9%; the analyst finds no compelling evidence of AI replacement.
limits: secondary summary of HESA data; one year's change

title: UK entry-level job postings since ChatGPT
measure: Entry-level job adverts (% change since Nov 2022)
finding: UK entry-level adverts were reported about 30% lower than at ChatGPT's launch, during a period of higher employer NICs and minimum-wage rises.
limits: second-hand (Adzuna via press); not split by exposure

cite: Bank of Korea (Oh Sam-il, labour market team) 2026
title: Youth job losses concentrated in AI-exposed industries (as reported)
measure: Change in employment of 15–29 year olds by industry AI exposure, Jun 2022–Jun 2026
finding: Of 285,000 youth jobs lost in South Korea from June 2022 to June 2026, 268,000 (94%) were in high-AI-exposure industries, while workers in their 50s gained 230,000 jobs.
limits: read via newspaper, not BOK page; correlational; BOK says not attributable to AI alone

title: Active Tech Jobs Outlook, India
measure: Active tech job openings by experience band (count)
finding: Entry-level tech openings in India fell 44% year on year to June 2026; the report does not cite AI.
limits: staffing firm, trade press; method unknown

cite: SurePoint Law School Hiring Report via Artificial Lawyer 2026
title: New associate hires at AmLaw 200 firms
measure: New associates hired by AmLaw 200 firms (count per year)
finding: Big-law entry hiring has been flat at about 7,400–7,600 a year since 2022 while laterals now outnumber new hires.
limits: second-hand; vendor report; flat trend predates legal AI

title: Are businesses scaling back hiring due to AI?
measure: Share of regional firms reporting AI-related lay-offs / reduced hiring (past 6 months)
latest_value: 1% of service firms laid off due to AI; 12% scaled back hiring; 11% hired more (2025)
finding: Only 1% of New York-region service firms reported AI lay-offs, while 12% reported hiring less because of AI.
limits: regional; self-report

title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? (Aug 2026 revision): No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%
measure: Shortfall vs 'kept pace' counterfactual for 22–25 year olds in highly exposed occupations (%)
finding: The shortfall widened from 15% (Jul 2025 data) to 19% (Jun 2026), surviving rate and remote-work controls but shrinking when education is accounted for.
limits: descriptive; headline measure changed between versions

title: Canaries, Interest Rates, and Timing
measure: Relative employment of young workers by AI and interest-rate exposure; firm-time fixed effects
finding: AI-exposed jobs are on average less rate-sensitive; with firm-time fixed effects the young-worker decline appears only from 2024 and reaches about 16% by Oct 2025.
limits: rate exposure data coarse and not by age

title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change (May 2026 version)
measure: Junior vs senior employment in GenAI-adopting vs non-adopting firms (Revelio résumé and posting data, ~281,000 firms, 2015–2025)
finding: Junior employment fell about 9% after six quarters in adopting firms relative to non-adopters (8% after eight quarters in an event study), through slower hiring, with senior employment unchanged.
limits: adoption inferred from postings; online-profile data; working paper

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market (NBER w33509)
measure: Labour demand by task AI exposure within firms, 2010–2023
finding: AI-exposed tasks see reduced labour demand, but productivity gains at adopting firms offset it, so overall employment effects are modest.
limits: pre-generative AI/ML mostly; not age-specific

title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (NBER w33777)
measure: Earnings and hours of chatbot adopters vs others (survey linked to registers)
finding: Precise null effects on earnings and hours, ruling out effects above 2% two years after ChatGPT, while tasks are reorganised.
limits: incumbent workers only; cannot see missed first jobs

title: Early impact of AI on the UK job market (SSRN 5516798)
measure: Employment, junior positions and postings in highly AI-exposed firms/occupations, 2021–2025 (postings + LinkedIn profiles)
finding: Highly exposed UK firms cut employment 4.5%, concentrated in junior positions (−5.8%), and postings in highly exposed occupations fell 23.4%.
limits: news summary read, not paper; exposure-based

title: Graduating into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors
measure: Initial employment probability and earnings by major AI exposure (administrative records)
finding: Graduates of the most exposed tenth of majors were 5 points less likely to find a first job and earned 13% less, effects fading but substantial later.
limits: divergence starts late 2022 before firm adoption; not peer reviewed

title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
measure: Unemployment and job-finding rates by observed AI task coverage (CPS)
finding: No unemployment difference, but 22–25 year olds' job-finding into the most exposed occupations fell about 14% ('just barely' significant).
limits: vendor; fragile estimate

title: Artificial Intelligence Has Not Impacted Youth Labor Market Outcomes in Finland
measure: Youth employment and wage growth by AI exposure (income registers)
finding: No evidence of AI-driven displacement or slower wage growth for young Finnish workers; a modest youth employment fall is attributed to demographics.
limits: no figures on summary page; strong employment protection

title: Labor Market Consequences of Generative AI: Early Evidence from Norway
measure: Employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations, registers 2015–Mar 2025
finding: No robust displacement of young workers; coefficients negative but small and insignificant, and backdating suggests pre-existing trends.
limits: data end Mar 2025

title: Has AI Widened Employment Gaps? Tracking Early-Career Employment by Occupational Exposure in Norway
measure: Private-sector employment by exposure quintile and age, Jan 2021–Feb 2026 (A-ordningen)
finding: Most exposed occupations grew 0.1% vs 0.3% for least exposed since Oct 2022; for 21–30 year olds the gap is an imprecise zero, but a 22–25 replication shows an emerging gap of about 35 log points by Feb 2026 (not significant; pre-trends rejected).
limits: emerging, not identified; small cells

title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative AI on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
measure: Monthly jobs and earnings of Upwork writing and image freelancers
finding: After ChatGPT, writing freelancers' monthly jobs fell about 2% and earnings 5.2%; top-rated freelancers were not protected.
limits: 2022–23 only; freelance is a small share of work

title: Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms (Management Science)
measure: Freelance job posts by automation-prone category
finding: Posts for automation-prone writing and coding jobs fell 21% within eight months of ChatGPT, and image-creation posts 17%; remaining posts were more complex and better paid.
limits: one platform; 2022–23

title: Winners and Losers of Generative AI: Early Evidence of Shifts in Freelancer Demand (JEBO)
measure: Freelance demand by skill cluster (substitutable vs complementary)
finding: Demand for substitutable skills such as writing and translation fell 20–50% against trend, and demand for novice workers declined.
limits: one platform; GPT-4o classification

title: Lost in translation: AI's impact on translators and foreign language skills
measure: Translator employment growth vs machine-translation use, 696 local labour markets, 2010–2023
finding: Each 1-point rise in machine-translation use cut translator employment growth by about 0.7 points, roughly 28,000 fewer new translator jobs.
limits: pre-LLM machine translation; growth not levels

title: Remote Work Leaves Younger Workers Sidelined
measure: Unemployment of young vs experienced graduates in remotable vs non-remotable occupations
finding: Remote work explains about 64% of the rise in young-graduate unemployment from 2017–19 to 2022–24; AI exposure does not explain the bulk.
limits: back-of-envelope; data end 2024

title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor-Market Effects of AI?
measure: Postings in high vs low AI-exposure occupations, junior vs senior
finding: The relative fall in exposed-occupation postings began before ChatGPT with no extra break after, and junior and senior postings moved in parallel.
limits: postings not hires

title: Looking for the Ladder: Is AI Impacting Entry-Level Jobs?
measure: Lightcast postings by AI-exposure quintile and seniority, Sep 2019–Aug 2025
finding: Exposed-occupation postings peaked in Mar–Apr 2022 with the first rate rise; junior and senior postings fell in parallel, and a hiring freeze mechanically hits 22–25s hardest.
limits: authors are Google economists; data to Aug 2025

title: AI and Young-adult Jobs: The Real Mystery
measure: Employment rates of 22–25 year olds with and without degrees (CPS)
finding: Employment rates fell for young adults with and without degrees, slightly more for non-graduates, so the puzzle is young people of all types.
limits: blog; figures only in charts

title: Class of 2026: young college graduates face a weaker labor market, but a more mixed picture
measure: Unemployment and employment rates, ages 22–27, graduates vs non-graduates (12-month averages)
finding: Young graduates' unemployment rose 1.3 points (Jul 2023–Mar 2026) but their employment rate held steady, 98% of the rise being more people looking; non-graduates rose 1.2 points.
limits: blog; not tied to AI

title: Are Young College Graduates Losing Their Edge in the Job Market?
measure: Job-finding (exit) rates of college vs high-school graduates since 1976
finding: Graduates' job-finding rate has fallen since about 2000 (47.0% average 1976–2000 to 37.1% in the year to Jun 2025), which AI cannot explain.
limits: long-run, not AI-specific

title: Young workers' employment drops in occupations with high AI exposure
measure: Share of 20–24 year olds' employment in most exposed occupations (CPS)
finding: The share fell from 16.4% (Nov 2022) to 15.5% (Sep 2025); even if all became unemployment it would add only about 0.1 point to the aggregate rate.
limits: CPS noise; may reflect education

title: Is AI contributing to rising unemployment? Evidence from occupational variation
measure: Correlation of occupation AI exposure/adoption with unemployment change, 2022–2025
finding: Occupations more exposed to AI saw larger unemployment rises (correlation 0.47; 0.57 using actual adoption).
limits: correlation; one window

title: What is really happening to jobs? Separating AI hype from reality
measure: Unemployment change by AI-exposure quintile since 2022 (IPUMS-CPS, updating Eckhardt & Goldschlag 2025)
finding: Unemployment rose 0.77 points for the most exposed fifth and 0.85 for the least exposed since 2022, while entry-level hiring in exposed occupations 'clearly declined' around 2022.
limits: unemployment misses never-hired entrants

title: AI and Jobs: The Final Word (Until the Next One)
measure: Unemployment change by AI-exposure quintile (CPS)
finding: From 2022 to early 2025 unemployment rose 0.30 points for the most exposed fifth vs 0.94 for the least exposed.
limits: one-off; not age-specific

title: Worker Types, AI Exposure and the Recent Decline in Job-Finding Rates
measure: Job-finding rates by latent worker type and AI exposure (CPS flows)
finding: Highly AI-exposed occupations saw the largest falls in job-finding since 2023; new entrants' job-finding fell only modestly relative to job losers and leavers.
limits: no age split; no exposure figures in brief

title: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs
measure: Occupational dissimilarity index since ChatGPT vs internet era; exposure group shares
finding: The occupational mix changed only about 1 point faster than in the internet era; recent-graduate vs older dissimilarity stayed in a 30–33% band since 2021.
limits: small CPS samples; economy-wide

title: Is AI Responsible for the Rise in Entry-Level Unemployment?
measure: Entry-level postings by AI exposure since Jan 2023
finding: Entry-level postings fell over 35% since Jan 2023 (over 40% high-exposure vs 33% low-exposure); a 10-point rise in exposure goes with 11% less entry-level demand.
limits: vendor; baseline near end of hiring boom

cite: Burning Glass Institute (Levanon, Sigelman et al.) 2025
title: No Country for Young Grads
measure: Graduate unemployment/underemployment and entry-level hiring (report)
finding: Argues the young-graduate squeeze is structural, driven by an AI 'expertise upheaval', lean post-pandemic staffing and a graduate glut.
limits: figures in PDF not read; attribution not quantified

title: State of Talent Report 2025
measure: New-graduate share of Big Tech and startup hires (LinkedIn-type profiles)
finding: New-graduate hires at Big Tech fell over 50% from 2019 to 2024 and were 7% of hires.
limits: venture firm; tech only; not re-read

title: 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer
measure: Entry-level postings demanding senior-type skills vs others
finding: US entry-level roles demanding senior-type skills grew 35% (2019–2025) while other entry-level roles fell 10%.
limits: consultancy; method unpublished; not re-read

title: Employment at firms adopting enterprise AI (as cited by SIEPR)
measure: Employment growth after enterprise-AI adoption (card-spend data)
finding: Employment grew 10% in the two years after firms adopted enterprise AI, led by the heaviest spenders.
limits: second-hand; selection of growing firms; not age-specific

title: How will AI affect the global workforce?
measure: Share of US workers displaced if AI widely adopted; transition unemployment
finding: Baseline 6–7% of US workers displaced (range 3–14%), adding about 0.5 point to unemployment for about two years; unemployment of 20–30 year olds in tech-exposed jobs up almost 3 points since start of 2025.
limits: no date for transition; bank research

title: New Skills and AI Are Reshaping the Future of Work
measure: Employment in AI-vulnerable occupations by regional AI-skill demand
finding: In regions with high AI-skill demand, employment in AI-vulnerable occupations is 3.6% lower after five years; about 40% of global jobs exposed.
limits: not age-specific; blog summary

title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
measure: Share of jobs exposed to AI
finding: About 40% of global jobs and 60% in advanced economies are exposed, roughly half of which may be harmed.
limits: exposure, not displacement

title: Recent-graduate unemployment and underemployment, 2030/2035
measure: Community forecast of recent-graduate unemployment and underemployment
finding: Forecasters expect recent-graduate unemployment of 10% by 2030 and 11.9% by 2035 (5.5% in 2025), and underemployment of 48.4% by 2030.
limits: crowd forecast; not re-read this session

title: Economists' forecasts of youth unemployment under AI scenarios
measure: US youth (20–24) unemployment rate in 2030 by AI scenario
finding: Median economist forecast for 2030 youth unemployment is 9.5% unconditional, 11.0% under rapid AI progress.
limits: medians only; not re-read

title: AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs
measure: Entry-level white-collar jobs eliminated; unemployment 10–20% within 1–5 years
finding: An AI-company CEO claims AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years.
limits: outlier; interested party

title: Future of Jobs Report 2025
measure: Jobs created and displaced 2025–2030 (employer survey)
finding: Employers expect 170m jobs created and 92m displaced worldwide by 2030 (net +78m).
limits: employer expectations; all technologies

title: Measuring the Economic Effects of AI: A path forward
measure: Proposed official metrics: occupation in QWI hires/separations; PSEO graduate cohorts; yearly ABS and frequent BTOS AI modules; AI items in JOLTS and CPS
finding: Proposes adding occupation to Census QWI and linking firm AI use to hires and separations so young workers in exposed jobs can be tracked in administrative data.
limits: proposal only

title: AI Economic Indicators (Canaries Dashboard, Transformation Tracker)
measure: Monthly canaries series plus 12-indicator macro transformation check
finding: Stanford's macro tracker finds 'no decisive evidence of transformation' apart from a rising capital share (Jul 2026).
limits: tracker verdicts qualitative

title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
measure: Review of confounders (over-hiring, rates, remote work) and exposure-measure sensitivity
finding: Results are sensitive to which AI exposure measure is used and confounded by over-hiring, rates and remote work.
limits: not re-read this session
